scenes.narration: The legacy of David Ben-Gurion outlived the circumstances that produced it. As head of the Jewish Agency from 1935, and later president of the Jewish Agency Executive, he was the de facto leader of the Jewish community in Palestine, and largely led the movement for an independent Jewish state in Mandatory Palestine. Born in Płońsk, then part of Congress Poland, to Polish Jewish parents, he immigrated to the Palestine region of the Ottoman Empire in 1906.

Few lives travel as far as that of David Ben-Gurion, and the distance is the point. Adopting the name of Ben-Gurion in 1909, he rose to become the preeminent leader of the Jewish community in British-ruled Mandatory Palestine from 1935 until the establishment of the State of Israel in 1948, which he led until 1963 with a short break in 1954–55. Ben-Gurion's interest for Zionism developed early in his life, leading him to become a major Zionist leader, and the executive head of the World Zionist Organization in 1946.

The childhood of David Ben-Gurion contains the adult in small print. On 14 May 1948, he formally proclaimed the establishment of Israel, and was the first to sign the Israeli Declaration of Independence, which he had helped to write. Under Ben-Gurion's leadership, the 1948 Arab–Israeli War saw the uniting of the various Jewish militias into the Israel Defense Forces (IDF), the victory of Israel over the Arab League, and the expulsion and flight of a majority of the Palestinian Arab population.

Money, luck and timing all played their parts in the life of David Ben-Gurion — in that order. Following the war, Ben-Gurion served as Israel's first prime minister and minister of defence. As prime minister, he helped build state institutions, presiding over national projects aimed at the development of the country.

The turning point in the life of David Ben-Gurion looked like a failure at the time. A major part of his foreign policy was improving relations with West Germany through a reparations agreement in compensation for Nazi confiscation of Jewish property during the Holocaust. In 1954, he resigned as prime minister and minister of defence but remained a member of the Knesset.

Every biography of David Ben-Gurion has to pass through the years that were quietly lost. He returned as minister of defence in 1955 after the Lavon Affair and the resignation of Pinhas Lavon. Later that year he became prime minister again, following the 1955 elections.

The education of David Ben-Gurion happened mostly outside any school. He backed Israel's reprisal operations to Arab guerrilla attacks and its invasion of Egypt, along with Britain and France, during the Suez Crisis in 1956. He then moved to his modest "hut" in Sde Boker, a kibbutz in the Negev desert, where he lived until his death.

What David Ben-Gurion wanted at the start and what David Ben-Gurion got are not the same thing, and that gap is the story. Posthumously, Ben-Gurion was named one of Time magazine's 100 Most Important People of the 20th century. David Ben-Gurion was born in Płońsk in Congress Poland—then part of the Russian Empire, to Polish Jewish parents.

The defining trait of David Ben-Gurion was not talent — it was the refusal to stop. His father, Avigdor Grün, was a court scribe and an unofficial legal adviser, writing petitions for his clients within the often corrupt Imperial legal system. Following the publication of Theodor Herzl's Der Judenstaat in 1896 Avigdor co-founded a Zionist group called Beni Zion—Children of Zion.

Those who met David Ben-Gurion at the peak describe someone still running on the early hunger. David was the youngest of three boys with an older and younger sister. Ben-Gurion's birth certificate, found in Poland in 2003, indicated that he had a twin brother who died shortly after birth.

The private years of David Ben-Gurion explain the public decades better than any speech. Between the ages of five and 13 Ben-Gurion attended five different heders as well as compulsory Russian classes. Two of the heders were 'modern' and taught in Hebrew rather than Yiddish.

The family David Ben-Gurion came from matters more than the legends admit. His father could not afford to enrol Ben-Gurion in Płońsk's beth midrash so Ben-Gurion's formal education ended after his bar mitzvah. At the age of 14 he and two friends formed a youth club, Ezra, promoting Hebrew studies and emigration to the Holy Land.

The first real success of David Ben-Gurion arrived later than anyone expected, and changed everything. The group ran Hebrew classes for local youth and in 1903 collected funds for the victims of the Kishinev pogrom. A different source estimates the group never had more than "several dozen" members.

The last chapter of David Ben-Gurion was written long after the fame. In 1904 Ben-Gurion moved to Warsaw, where he hoped to enroll in the Warsaw Mechanical-Technical School founded by Hipolit Wawelberg. He did not have sufficient qualifications to matriculate and took work teaching Hebrew in a Warsaw heder.

The whole life of David Ben-Gurion reads like a single decision repeated. He became involved in Zionist politics and in October 1905 he joined the clandestine Social-Democratic Jewish Workers' Party—Poalei Zion. Two months later he was the delegate from Płońsk at a local conference.

Between the birth and the legend of David Ben-Gurion lie the years that actually decide it. While in Warsaw the Russian Revolution of 1905 broke out and he was in the city during the clampdown that followed; he was arrested twice, the second time he was held for two weeks and only released with the help of his father. In December 1905 he returned to Płońsk as a full-time Poalei Zion operative.

The reputation of David Ben-Gurion was built in the middle, not at the edges. There he worked to oppose the anti-Zionist Bund who were trying to establish a base. He was known to use intimidatory tactics, such as extorting money from wealthy Jews at gunpoint to raise funds for Jewish workers.

Somebody like David Ben-Gurion should not have made it — that is exactly why the story survives. Nevertheless, and I think this very significant, it was Płońsk that sent the highest proportion of Jews to Eretz Israel from any town in Poland of comparable size. We emigrated not for negative reasons of escape but for the positive purpose of rebuilding a homeland ...

The life of David Ben-Gurion begins far from where the story usually starts. The number of Jews and Poles in the city were roughly equal, about five thousand each. The Jews, however, formed a compact, centralized group occupying the innermost districts whilst the Poles were more scattered, living in outlying areas and shading off into the peasantry.

David Ben-Gurion was not born famous — the early years shaped everything that followed. Far from being afraid of them, they were rather afraid of us. He travelled with his sweetheart, Rachel Nelkin, and her mother, as well as Shlomo Zemach, his comrade from Ezra.

To understand where David Ben-Gurion ended up, start with where David Ben-Gurion began. Immediately on landing in Jaffa, 7 September 1906, Ben-Gurion set off, on foot, in a group of 14, to Petah Tikva. It was the largest of the 13 Jewish agricultural settlements and consisted of 80 households with a population of nearly 1,500; of these around 200 were Second Aliyah pioneers like Ben-Gurion.

The road from the beginning to the peak of David Ben-Gurion ran through years nobody filmed. He found work as a day labourer, waiting each morning hoping to be chosen by an overseer. Jewish workers found it difficult competing with local villagers who were more skilled and prepared to work for less.

Each stage of the life of David Ben-Gurion made the next stage possible. In November he caught malaria and the doctor advised he return to Europe. By the time he left Petah Tikva in summer of 1907 he had worked an average 10 days a month which frequently left him with no money for food.

The people who knew David Ben-Gurion young describe someone already restless. Others who had come from Płońsk were writing about tuberculosis, cholera and people dying of hunger. On his disembarkation at Jaffa, Ben-Gurion had been spotted by Israel Shochat who had arrived two years previously and had established a group of around 25 Poale Zion followers.

What David Ben-Gurion built in the middle years is what the name still stands for. A month after his arrival at Petah Tikva, Shochat invited Ben-Gurion to attend the founding conference of the Jewish Social Democratic Workers' Party in the Land of Israel in Jaffa. The conference, 4–6 October 1906, was attended by 60 or so people.

By the time David Ben-Gurion reached the defining moment, the preparation was decades old. Shochat engineered the elections so that Ben-Gurion was elected onto the five-man Central Committee and the 10-man Manifesto Committee. These Ben-Gurion conducted in Hebrew, forbidding the translation of his address into Russian or Yiddish.

The rise of David Ben-Gurion was not an accident — in retrospect the pattern is plain. The conference was divided: a large faction—Rostovians—wanted to create a single Arab–Jewish proletariat. The conference delegated the Manifesto Committee the task of deciding the new party's objectives.

Setbacks came early for David Ben-Gurion, and the response to them is the real story. They produced The Ramleh Programme which was approved by a second smaller 15-man conference held in Jaffa the following January 1907. The programme stated "the party aspires to political independence of the Jewish People in this country." All activities were to be conducted in Hebrew; there should be segregation of the Jewish and the Arab economies; and a Jewish trade union was to be established.

The legacy of David Ben-Gurion outlived the circumstances that produced it. Three members of the Central Committee resigned and Ben-Gurion and Shochat continued meeting weekly in Jaffa or Ben Shemen where Shochat was working. Ben-Gurion walked to the meetings from Petah Tikva until he moved to Jaffa where he gave occasional Hebrew lessons.

Few lives travel as far as that of David Ben-Gurion, and the distance is the point. His political activity resulted in the establishment of three small trade unions amongst some tailors, carpenters and shoemakers. He and Shochat also brokered a settlement to a strike at the Rishon Le Zion winery where six workers had been sacked.

The childhood of David Ben-Gurion contains the adult in small print. After three months the two-man Central Committee was dissolved, partly because, at that time, Ben-Gurion was less militant than Shochat and the Rostovians. During this time Ben-Gurion sent a letter to Yiddish Kemfer ("The Jewish Fighter"), a Yiddish newspaper in New York City.

Money, luck and timing all played their parts in the life of David Ben-Gurion — in that order. It was an appeal for funds and was the first time something written by Ben-Gurion was published. The arrival of Yitzhak Ben-Zvi in April 1907 revitalised the local Poale Zion.

The turning point in the life of David Ben-Gurion looked like a failure at the time. Eighty followers attended a conference in May at which Ben-Zvi was elected onto a two-man Central Committee and all Ben-Gurion's policies were reversed: Yiddish, not Hebrew, was the language to be used; the future lay with a united Jewish and Arab proletariat. Further disappointment came when Ben-Zvi and Shochat were elected as representatives to go to the World Zionist Congress.

Every biography of David Ben-Gurion has to pass through the years that were quietly lost. He was not aware that at the next gathering, on Ben-Zvi's return, a secret para-military group was set up—Bar-Giora—under Shochat's leadership. Distancing himself from Poale Zion activism Ben-Gurion, who had been a day-labourer at Kfar Saba, moved to Rishon Lezion where he remained for two months.
